He did not try again. The boys lay counting the moments as they slowly passed. It seemed as if time had ended and even eternity was growing old. At last, to their relief, they saw that the sun was setting.

One of the men stopped snoring. Injun Joe sat up and looked around. He gave a grim smile at his companion, whose head hung over his knees, then nudged him awake with his foot.

“Hey! Some watchman you are! Still, it's all right. Nothing's happened.”

“Goodness! Have I been asleep?”

“Oh, a bit, a bit. It's nearly time to get moving, partner. What should we do with the little stolen money we've got left?”

“I don't know. Leave it here like we always do, I suppose. No point taking it away until we head south. Six hundred and fifty dollars in silver is heavy to carry.”

“Well, all right. Coming back here once more won't matter.”

“No, but I'd come at night, like before. That's safer.”

“Yes, but listen. It may be a long time before I get my chance at that job. Something could go wrong, and this isn't a very good hiding place. Let's bury it properly, deep in the ground.”

“Good idea,” his companion said. He crossed the room, knelt, and lifted a stone at the back of the fireplace. Beneath it was a bag that jingled pleasantly as he pulled it out. He took twenty or thirty dollars for himself and the same for Injun Joe. Then he handed the bag to Joe, who was now kneeling in the corner, digging with his large bowie-knife.

The boys instantly forgot their fear and misery. They watched every movement with hungry eyes. What luck! It was more wonderful than anything they could have imagined. Six hundred dollars could make half a dozen boys rich! This was treasure-hunting under perfect conditions. There would be no frustrating uncertainty about where to dig. They kept nudging each other, and every nudge said clearly, “Aren't you glad we're here now?”

Joe's knife hit something.

“What's this?” he said.

“What is it?” his companion asked.

“A half-rotten plank. No, I think it's a box. Here, give me a hand and we'll see what it's doing here. Never mind, I've broken a hole in it.”

He reached inside and brought his hand out.

“Man, it's money!”

The two men examined the handful of coins. They were gold. The boys upstairs were just as excited and delighted as they were.

Joe's companion said:

“We'll soon get this out. There's an old rusty pick in the weeds in the corner on the other side of the fireplace. I noticed it a minute ago.”

When I was young, I never felt dissatisfied with life. Even if boredom overcame me, the beauty of nature or the study of humanity's finest, most inspiring creations could always capture my interest and lift my spirits. But now I am like a tree struck by lightning: the blow has reached my soul. I felt then that I would live on only to become what I will soon cease to be—a miserable example of a ruined human being, pitiful to others and unbearable to myself.

We spent a good deal of time at Oxford, walking through the surrounding countryside and trying to identify every place connected with the most stirring period of English history. Often our little trips of discovery grew longer as one interesting sight led to another. We visited the great Hampden's tomb and the field where that patriot fell. For a moment, these places lifted my mind above its degrading fears and misery. They reminded me of the noble ideals of freedom and self-sacrifice, which I paused to consider. For an instant I dared to shake off my chains and look around with a free and uplifted spirit. But the iron had cut too deeply into my flesh. Trembling and without hope, I sank back into my miserable self.

We were sorry to leave Oxford and continued to Matlock, our next stopping place. The countryside near this village looked more like Switzerland, although everything was smaller. The green hills lacked the distant crown of white Alps that always rises beyond the pine-covered mountains of my homeland. We visited the wonderful cave and the small natural-history collections. Their unusual objects were arranged in the same way as those at Servox and Chamounix. When Henry said the name Chamounix, I trembled. I hurried to leave Matlock, now linked in my mind with that terrible scene.

From Derby we continued north and spent two months in Cumberland and Westmorland. Here I could almost imagine myself back among the Swiss mountains. Small patches of snow still lay on the mountains' northern slopes. The lakes and the streams rushing over rocks were familiar, beloved sights. We also met some people whose company almost persuaded me to be happy. Clerval's pleasure was greater than mine in proportion to our different spirits. His mind grew in the company of talented men. He discovered abilities and resources within himself far beyond anything he had imagined possessing when he had lived among people less gifted than himself.

All the young people were eager to visit Lyme. Captain Wentworth spoke of going back there himself. It was only seventeen miles from Uppercross, and although it was November, the weather was quite good. Louisa, the most eager of them all, had made up her mind to go. Besides enjoying getting her own way, she now believed there was virtue in sticking to a decision. She overcame all her parents' wishes to delay the visit until summer. So Lyme it would be, with Charles, Mary, Anne, Henrietta, Louisa, and Captain Wentworth making the trip.

Their first careless plan was to leave in the morning and return that night. But Mr. Musgrove would not agree, out of concern for his horses. Once they thought it through sensibly, they realized that a mid-November day would leave little time to explore a new place. Given the countryside they had to cross, the journey there and back would take seven hours. They therefore decided to stay overnight and return in time for dinner the next day. Everyone felt this was a considerable improvement. They met for an unusually early breakfast at the Great House and set off exactly on time. Even so, it was well past noon when the two carriages descended the long hill into Lyme and entered the town's even steeper main street. The four ladies traveled in Mr. Musgrove's coach, while Charles drove Captain Wentworth in his two-wheeled carriage. Clearly, they would have only enough time to look around before the day's light and warmth disappeared.

Once they had arranged rooms and ordered dinner at an inn, there could be no doubt about what to do next: walk straight down to the sea. They had arrived too late in the year to enjoy the entertainments and variety Lyme offered as a resort. The assembly rooms were closed, almost all the visitors had left their lodgings, and scarcely any families remained apart from permanent residents. The buildings themselves have little to admire. Instead, a visitor looks at the town's striking position, with its main street seeming almost to rush into the water; the walk to the Cobb around the pleasant little bay, crowded in the season with people and wheeled bathing huts; and the Cobb itself, with its old marvels and recent improvements. There is also the beautiful line of cliffs stretching eastward from the town. A visitor would be strange indeed who found nothing attractive in Lyme's immediate surroundings to make them want to become better acquainted with it.
